title: There are several Screams
hook: Edvard Munch made The Scream several times, in paint, pastel, crayon and print.
peek: There is no single Scream. Edvard Munch made the image again and again: a painting, a crayon drawing, two pastels, a later painted version and a lithograph that was printed many times. Two museums in Oslo hold most of them.
lede: Most people picture The Scream as one painting in one museum. In fact Edvard Munch returned to the image several times. There is a painted version from 1893, a crayon version from the same year, two pastels, a lithograph from 1895 that could be printed in many copies, and a second painted version usually dated to around 1910. Each one is a genuine Scream.

bullets.text: The best known version, in tempera and crayon on cardboard, belongs to Norway's National Museum in Oslo. It is the one most often reproduced on posters and mugs.

One pastel stayed in private hands for over a century. Its frame carries a poem Munch wrote about the scene. In 2012 it sold at auction in New York for about 120 million dollars, then a record for a work of art.
In 1895 Munch drew the image on a lithographic stone, so it could be printed in black and white. That print spread the picture far more widely than any single painting could.

Munch's original German title was Der Schrei der Natur, The Scream of Nature. He described walking at sunset and sensing a great scream passing through nature, so the figure is often read as hearing the scream rather than making it.
